idiom_name: closure parameter, @escaping for stored completion handlers; checked continuations to bridge
implementation_notes: Closures are the callback form, and @escaping marks the ones the callee stores and calls after returning (URLSession completion handlers, DispatchQueue.async, Timer), which is exactly the deferred-callback contract; non-escaping closures are guaranteed to run within the call. The modern replacement is async/await - the operation becomes an async function and callback-based APIs are bridged with withCheckedContinuation/withCheckedThrowingContinuation - while completion handlers remain right where the callback fires more than once (progress, streams) or must stay at an Objective-C/framework boundary. A single-method protocol is the classic shape and is still preferred for multi-method delegates with identity.
pitfalls: An escaping closure that captures self strongly creates a retain cycle whenever the callee is owned by that same object; the URLSession completion handler is the classic case, fixed with [weak self].
Completion handlers run on the callee's queue, not the caller's, so UI work must hop to the main actor and shared state needs isolation.
Checked continuations trap on a second resume and warn when leaked, so bridging an API that may call back twice (or never) requires an atomic guard around the continuation.
@escaping is never implied: storing or dispatching a non-escaping closure is a compile error, so the distinction has to be designed into the API rather than added later.
